questions.stem: An 81 year old retired teacher is brought to her GP by her son. Over 3 years she has gradually become more forgetful, repeats the same questions and recently got lost driving to her local shop. She now needs help paying bills. Neurological examination is normal and there is no history of stroke. Her MMSE score is 19/30.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Gradual, progressive memory loss affecting daily function with a normal neurological examination is Alzheimer's disease, the commonest dementia.

steps.x: Slow, smooth decline in memory with loss of daily function and no focal signs.

elim: No fluctuation, hallucinations or parkinsonism.
Memory loss came first and she is 81; FTD starts younger with behaviour change.
No gait disturbance or urinary incontinence.
No stroke history, no focal signs and the decline is gradual, not stepwise.

steps.x: A: Alzheimer's disease. Gradual memory-first decline with normal neurology = Alzheimer's.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man with atrial fibrillation, hypertension and a stroke 3 years ago is reviewed in clinic. His wife says his memory was stable for a year, then dropped suddenly after a 'funny turn' 6 months ago, and dropped again last month. Examination shows a left pronator drift and brisk reflexes on the left. His MMSE score is 21/30.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Stepwise decline against a background of stroke and vascular risk factors, with focal neurological signs, is vascular dementia from cumulative ischaemic damage.

steps.x: Stepwise falls after vascular events plus focal signs.

elim: Smooth decline with normal neurology, not stepwise falls with focal signs.
No hallucinations, fluctuation or parkinsonism.
Behaviour-led and younger onset.
Depression does not produce focal neurological signs.

steps.x: E: Vascular dementia. Stepwise decline + strokes/TIAs + focal signs = vascular dementia.

questions.stem: A 54 year old accountant is brought in by his wife. Over 9 months he has made sexual comments to colleagues, eats whole packets of biscuits at a time and insists on walking the same route every day. He remembers recent events well. On cognitive testing he cannot copy a pair of interlocking pentagons.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A younger patient with early disinhibition, compulsions, binge eating and constructional apraxia but preserved memory has frontotemporal dementia.

steps.x: Young onset, disinhibition, compulsions and binge eating with memory spared.

elim: Memory is relatively preserved here; Alzheimer's starts with memory loss in older people.
No fluctuation, hallucinations or parkinsonism.
No gait or bladder disturbance.
No stroke history or stepwise course.

steps.x: C: Frontotemporal dementia. Behaviour first, memory spared, under 65 = FTD.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man is brought to clinic by his daughter. Over 10 months his thinking has been clear on some days and muddled on others. He describes small children sitting on the end of his bed at night. In the last 2 months he has started to shuffle and his handwriting has become small. His MMSE score varies between 18 and 25.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fluctuating cognition, Lilliputian visual hallucinations and later parkinsonism are the core triad of dementia with Lewy bodies.

clues: clear on some days and muddled on others
small children sitting on the end of his bed
steps.x: Fluctuating cognition, small-people hallucinations, then parkinsonism.

elim: Does not cause marked day-to-day fluctuation and early visual hallucinations.
Develops over hours to days, not 10 months.
Parkinsonism would come at least a year before the dementia, not after it.
No stroke history or focal signs.

steps.x: C: Dementia with Lewy bodies. Fluctuation + hallucinations + parkinsonism = DLB.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has been diagnosed with dementia with Lewy bodies. Her husband is asked about other symptoms she may have developed over the past few years. Her blood pressure is 142/84 mmHg lying and 112/70 mmHg standing.
questions.q: Which other feature is she most likely to have?
o: Acting out her dreams while asleep
Early urinary incontinence with a magnetic gait
Loose stools several times a day
questions.e: REM sleep behaviour disorder is a recognised feature of DLB, alongside falls, anosmia and autonomic dysfunction such as postural hypotension and constipation.

steps.x: DLB with postural hypotension: think of its other non-cognitive features.

elim: Triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus.
DLB causes anosmia, not heightened smell.
DLB autonomic dysfunction causes constipation.
Typical of frontotemporal dementia.

steps.x: A: Acting out her dreams while asleep. DLB extras: REM sleep disorder, falls, anosmia, constipation, dizziness.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man is brought to his GP by his daughter, who thinks he has dementia. Since his wife died 4 months ago he has lost 6 kg, stopped washing and says he cannot concentrate on the newspaper. During testing he often answers 'I don't know' but scores 29/30 on the MMSE. Physical examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Severe depression after bereavement causes poor concentration, self-neglect and weight loss that mimics dementia, but the MMSE is typically normal.

steps.x: Bereavement, weight loss, 'don't know' answers and a normal MMSE.

elim: Would give a low MMSE score with gradual decline over years.
No acute fluctuating confusion or physical trigger.
No disinhibition or compulsions; onset follows bereavement.
No vascular history or stepwise course.

steps.x: C: Depressive pseudodementia. Apparent impairment with a normal MMSE = pseudodementia (depression).

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman has had 8 months of worsening memory. Her husband says she now walks as if her feet are stuck to the floor, with short, broad-based steps, and she has started wetting herself before reaching the toilet. Power, tone and reflexes are normal. There is no tremor.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Urinary incontinence, gait disturbance and dementia together ('wet, wobbly and wacky') is normal pressure hydrocephalus.

clues: walks as if her feet are stuck to the floor
steps.x: Magnetic gait, urinary incontinence and cognitive decline.

elim: Does not cause early gait disturbance and urinary incontinence.
No fluctuation or hallucinations, and no tremor or rigidity.
No tremor, rigidity or bradykinesia; incontinence is early here.
No stroke history or focal signs.

steps.x: C: Normal pressure hydrocephalus. Wet, wobbly and wacky = normal pressure hydrocephalus.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman with Down syndrome lives in a group home. Over 18 months her carers report she has lost skills she once had: she can no longer make a cup of tea, has become withdrawn and forgets the names of staff. Thyroid function tests, B12 and folate are normal. There is no low mood or weight loss.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Down syndrome is a strong risk factor for early-onset Alzheimer's disease, presenting with loss of previously acquired skills and memory.

clues: Thyroid function tests, B12 and folate are normal
steps.x: Down syndrome with loss of skills and memory; reversible causes excluded.

elim: No low mood, weight loss or bereavement trigger.
Disinhibition and compulsions would lead, with memory spared.
Thyroid function tests are normal.
No gait disturbance or incontinence.

steps.x: A: Alzheimer's disease. Down syndrome + cognitive decline in mid-life = early-onset Alzheimer's.

questions.stem: An 86 year old woman with Alzheimer's disease lives in a care home. Over 2 days she has become much more confused, is drowsy in the morning and agitated at night and keeps pulling at her clothes. Her temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. Urine dipstick is positive for nitrites and leucocytes.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An acute, fluctuating worsening over days with infection in someone with dementia is delirium, an emergency superimposed on the underlying dementia.

clues: drowsy in the morning and agitated at night
steps.x: Acute fluctuating confusion with a urinary infection.

elim: A 2-day change with fever and a urinary source is acute, not a new chronic dementia.
Does not cause acute fluctuating drowsiness with fever.
Alzheimer's progresses over months to years, not days.
No stroke-like event or focal signs.

steps.x: A: Delirium superimposed on dementia. Sudden worsening in dementia = look for delirium and its cause.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man has had episodes of vivid visual hallucinations and periods of staring blankly for over a year. His wife says his memory and attention began to fail before any physical problems. Over the last 6 months he has developed a slow, shuffling gait and cogwheel rigidity in both arms.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: When cognitive problems and hallucinations come before or within a year of parkinsonism it is DLB; it sits on a spectrum with Parkinson's disease dementia, both caused by alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies.

clues: memory and attention began to fail before any physical problems
steps.x: Cognition and hallucinations first, parkinsonism later.

elim: Hallucinations and parkinsonism are not early features.
Behavioural change and disinhibition, not hallucinations and rigidity.
No incontinence; rigidity is not part of NPH.
Parkinsonism comes first, with dementia over a year later.

steps.x: B: Dementia with Lewy bodies. Dementia first then parkinsonism = DLB; parkinsonism first = PDD.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman has an 18 month history of personality change. She has become rude, laughs at funerals and has started shoplifting sweets. Her husband says she still remembers appointments and conversations. Her MoCA shows marked problems with verbal fluency and planning.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on further cognitive testing?
o: Marked fluctuation in attention through the day
Normal test results with 'I don't know' answers
questions.e: Frontotemporal dementia causes constructional apraxia (failing to copy interlocking pentagons) and executive problems, while memory is spared because the posterior cortex is preserved.

steps.x: Behaviour change with preserved memory: frontotemporal dementia.

elim: A core feature of DLB, not FTD.
Fluctuation suggests DLB or delirium.
Typical of depressive pseudodementia.
Memory is relatively preserved in early FTD.

steps.x: A: Inability to copy interlocking pentagons. FTD: constructional apraxia and executive dysfunction, memory relatively preserved.

questions.stem: An 80 year old man with type 2 diabetes, hypertension and two previous TIAs has a 2 year history of memory problems that worsen in steps. His wife says he has also had a few falls. His BP is 168/94 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Cogwheel rigidity with a resting tremor
Extensor plantar response on the right
questions.e: Vascular dementia from previous strokes or TIAs often comes with focal neurological signs such as an upgoing plantar.

steps.x: Vascular risk factors, TIAs and a stepwise course point to vascular dementia.

elim: Suggests parkinsonism, as in DLB.
Suggests motor neurone disease, as seen with FTD-ALS.
Expected in early Alzheimer's, not stepwise vascular disease.
Suggests raised intracranial pressure, not vascular dementia.

steps.x: B: Extensor plantar response on the right. Vascular dementia: expect focal neurological signs.

questions.stem: A 78 year old woman with known dementia with Lewy bodies is admitted with pneumonia. On her second night she is agitated and seeing animals in the room. A junior doctor gives oral haloperidol. The next morning she is very stiff, cannot get out of bed and has fallen twice.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her deterioration?
o: Antipsychotic sensitivity in dementia with Lewy bodies
questions.e: Antipsychotics such as haloperidol worsen parkinsonism in DLB and increase mortality, so they must be avoided.

steps.x: DLB plus haloperidol, then sudden rigidity and falls.

elim: No focal deficit; generalised rigidity after haloperidol.
Does not explain sudden severe rigidity after an antipsychotic.
Does not appear overnight.
Disease progression is gradual, not overnight after a drug.

steps.x: A: Antipsychotic sensitivity in dementia with Lewy bodies. Never give haloperidol in DLB: severe antipsychotic sensitivity.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has 2 years of disinhibition, apathy and compulsive eating. Over the last 6 months he has developed wasting of the hand muscles, fasciculations in both arms and slurred speech. His father had a similar illness.
questions.q: Which genetic abnormality is most likely?
questions.e: Frontotemporal dementia with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (behaviour change plus lower motor neurone signs) is linked to the C9orf72 gene.

steps.x: Familial FTD plus motor neurone disease.

elim: A risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease.
Causes Huntington's disease with chorea.
Causes familial early-onset Alzheimer's disease.
Down syndrome, linked to early Alzheimer's.

steps.x: B: C9orf72 repeat expansion. FTD + ALS in a family = C9orf72.

questions.stem: A 75 year old woman sees her GP with her daughter, who has noticed her mother forgetting conversations and missing appointments for a year. She lives alone and manages her own shopping with some help. Physical examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: The first step for suspected dementia is a validated cognitive assessment tool such as the MoCA, MMSE, 6CIT or Mini-Cog, alongside a confusion screen.

steps.x: A year of memory problems in primary care.

elim: Imaging comes after a cognitive assessment and bloods, usually via the memory clinic.
Used when dementia with Lewy bodies is suspected.
Not part of the routine dementia work-up.
Not a first-line test for suspected dementia.

steps.x: E: Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). First step in suspected dementia: a validated cognitive assessment tool.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has a 9 month history of slowed thinking, poor memory and weight gain. He feels cold all the time and his skin is dry. His 6CIT score suggests significant cognitive impairment. He is referred to the memory clinic.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to send at this stage?
questions.e: A confusion screen (including TFTs, FBC, U&Es, LFTs, haematinics, bone profile and glucose) is sent with the cognitive test to exclude reversible causes; this man's cold intolerance and weight gain suggest hypothyroidism.

steps.x: Cognitive decline with features of hypothyroidism.

elim: Not a routine test; reversible causes must be excluded first.
Only for suspected dementia with Lewy bodies.
Not part of the routine work-up.
For autoimmune encephalitis, not slow decline.

steps.x: E: Thyroid function tests. Always send a confusion screen to exclude reversible causes.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman has 1 year of fluctuating confusion, visual hallucinations of cats in the garden and recent falls. Examination shows mild bradykinesia. MRI brain shows mild generalised atrophy only. The memory clinic wants to confirm the subtype of dementia.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: A DaTscan (dopamine transporter SPECT) shows reduced uptake in the basal ganglia and is diagnostic for dementia with Lewy bodies.

steps.x: The DLB triad: fluctuation, hallucinations, parkinsonism.

elim: Adds nothing after a normal MRI.
Does not confirm dementia with Lewy bodies.
Used for normal pressure hydrocephalus, not DLB.
Delays the diagnosis without confirming the subtype.

steps.x: B: DaTscan (SPECT). Suspected DLB: DaTscan confirms it.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man has a 3 year history of gradually worsening memory with no focal neurological signs. His confusion screen is normal. His MoCA score is 17/30, with the worst scores in delayed recall. He has no tremor or gait problem. He has an MRI brain.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on MRI?
o: Bilateral temporal lobe high signal with oedema
Dilated ventricles out of proportion to sulci
Hippocampal and medial temporal lobe atrophy
Isolated frontal and anterior temporal atrophy
questions.e: In Alzheimer's disease plaques and tangles cause synaptic loss and cortical and hippocampal atrophy, seen on CT or MRI.

steps.x: Gradual memory-led decline: Alzheimer's.

elim: Suggests HSV encephalitis, an acute illness.
Suggests normal pressure hydrocephalus.
Suggests frontotemporal dementia.
Suggests vascular dementia.

steps.x: C: Hippocampal and medial temporal lobe atrophy. Alzheimer's imaging: hippocampal and cortical atrophy.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man has 1 year of slowing thinking, urinary urgency with incontinence and an unsteady, shuffling broad-based gait. CT head shows ventricles that are enlarged out of proportion to the cerebral sulci. There are no signs of raised intracranial pressure.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is investigated with lumbar puncture; improvement in gait after removing CSF predicts response to a shunt.

steps.x: Wet, wobbly and wacky with large ventricles.

elim: For suspected dementia with Lewy bodies.
Not used for this triad.
Gait is from the brain here; the triad points to the ventricles.
Treats the bladder symptom in isolation and misses the cause.

steps.x: C: Lumbar puncture. NPH: confirm with lumbar puncture, treat with VP shunt.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman has a year of progressive memory loss. Her MMSE is 20/30, her confusion screen is normal and a CT head shows generalised and hippocampal atrophy. Her son asks whether a single test can prove what is wrong.
questions.q: Which is the most accurate description of how this diagnosis is made?
o: Clinical diagnosis supported by brain imaging
CSF amyloid and tau levels in all patients
questions.e: Dementia is a clinical diagnosis from the history and cognitive testing, supported by imaging; there is no single confirmatory test.

steps.x: History, cognitive testing and imaging already point to Alzheimer's.

elim: Not done in life for routine dementia diagnosis.
Not a routine requirement in UK practice.
Only for dementia with Lewy bodies.
Not used to diagnose dementia.

steps.x: B: Clinical diagnosis supported by brain imaging. Dementia is a clinical diagnosis supported by imaging.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man has 1 year of apathy, disinhibited behaviour and loss of empathy towards his family. His memory and spatial navigation are preserved. His confusion screen is normal. He has an MRI brain.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on MRI?
o: Frontal and anterior temporal lobe atrophy
Hippocampal atrophy with posterior cortical loss
Ventricles dilated out of proportion to sulci
questions.e: FTD causes selective frontal and temporal atrophy that spares the posterior cortex, which is why memory and navigation are preserved early.

clues: memory and spatial navigation are preserved
steps.x: Behaviour-led dementia with preserved posterior functions.

elim: Typical of Alzheimer's disease.
Typical of vascular dementia.
FTD shows selective atrophy on MRI.
Suggests normal pressure hydrocephalus.

steps.x: A: Frontal and anterior temporal lobe atrophy. FTD imaging: frontotemporal atrophy, posterior cortex spared.

questions.stem: An 82 year old man with hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia and a 40 pack-year smoking history has a stepwise decline in memory and planning over 3 years, with mild left-sided weakness and a brisk left knee jerk. His confusion screen is normal and his MoCA score is 19/30.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on MRI brain?
o: Multiple infarcts with extensive white matter small vessel disease
Ventricles dilated out of proportion to sulci
questions.e: Vascular dementia results from cumulative ischaemic damage, either multiple infarcts or small vessel disease, seen on imaging.

steps.x: Vascular risk factors, stepwise course, focal weakness.

elim: Suggests HSV encephalitis.
Suggests frontotemporal dementia.
Suggests Alzheimer's disease.
Suggests normal pressure hydrocephalus.

steps.x: D: Multiple infarcts with extensive white matter small vessel disease. Vascular dementia imaging: infarcts and small vessel disease.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman is diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease at the memory clinic. Her MMSE score is 21/30. She takes amlodipine for hypertension. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and regular and an ECG shows sinus rhythm with a normal QT interval.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial drug treatment?
questions.e: First-line drug treatment for mild to moderate Alzheimer's is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, galantamine or rivastigmine).

steps.x: Mild-moderate Alzheimer's with no cardiac contraindication.

elim: An antipsychotic with no role in slowing cognitive decline.
Treats Parkinson's disease, not Alzheimer's.
Reserved for severe disease (MMSE under 10) or AChE inhibitor intolerance.
An SSRI for depression or FTD behaviour, not first-line for Alzheimer's.

steps.x: A: Donepezil. Mild-moderate Alzheimer's: start an AChE inhibitor.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man is diagnosed with moderate Alzheimer's disease. His MMSE score is 16/30. He has had dizzy spells and an ECG shows second-degree (Mobitz type II) heart block. He does not have a pacemaker. His pulse rate is 48 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate drug treatment for his dementia?
questions.e: AChE inhibitors are contraindicated in unpaced second or third-degree heart block, prolonged QT or bradycardia under 50 bpm, so memantine is substituted.

steps.x: Heart block and bradycardia rule out all AChE inhibitors.

elim: AChE inhibitors are contraindicated in unpaced heart block and bradycardia under 50 bpm.
Also an AChE inhibitor with the same contraindications.
An antipsychotic, not a dementia treatment.
Also an AChE inhibitor with the same contraindications.

steps.x: C: Memantine. AChE inhibitor contraindicated? Use memantine instead.

questions.stem: An 80 year old woman with Alzheimer's disease started rivastigmine 6 weeks ago. Her daughter reports she now has loose stools, nausea, drools more and has started leaking urine. Her pulse rate is 54 bpm. She has no fever and urine dipstick is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her new symptoms?
questions.e: AChE inhibitors cause cholinergic effects: diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting, bradycardia, increased salivation and urinary incontinence.

steps.x: New GI, salivary, bladder and heart rate effects after starting an AChE inhibitor.

elim: Causes dry mouth, constipation and retention, the opposite picture.
Does not cause diarrhoea, drooling or bradycardia.
Would not cause diarrhoea, drooling and bradycardia within weeks.
Dipstick is negative and there is no fever.

steps.x: B: Cholinergic side effects of rivastigmine. AChE inhibitors: diarrhoea, nausea, bradycardia, salivation, incontinence.

questions.stem: An 84 year old man with Alzheimer's disease has been on donepezil for 3 years. He now needs help with all personal care and rarely recognises his wife. His MMSE score is 8/30. He tolerates donepezil well and his ECG is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate change to his treatment?
o: Stop donepezil and give no further treatment
questions.e: In severe Alzheimer's (MMSE under 10), memantine, an NMDA receptor antagonist, is added; its main side effect is constipation.

steps.x: Severe Alzheimer's already on a tolerated AChE inhibitor.

elim: Antipsychotics are not used to treat cognitive decline.
Severe disease is an indication to add memantine, not withdraw treatment.
Anticholinergic and worsens cognition.
Changing AChE inhibitor does not address severe disease.

steps.x: B: Add memantine. Severe Alzheimer's (MMSE <10): add memantine.

questions.stem: An 82 year old woman with vascular dementia lives in a care home. Staff report that she has become agitated in the late afternoons, shouting and trying to leave the building. There is no evidence of pain, infection or constipation. She is not distressed at other times and is eating well.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management of her behaviour?
o: Person-centred care and support with environmental changes
questions.e: Care and support is first-line for behavioural symptoms in all dementias; drugs are kept for severe, distressing cases.

clues: no evidence of pain, infection or constipation
steps.x: Behavioural symptoms with physical causes excluded.

elim: Sedatives increase falls and confusion and are not first-line.
Drugs are reserved for severe cases after non-drug approaches.
Harmful and not an appropriate first step.
Not used for behaviour in vascular dementia.

steps.x: C: Person-centred care and support with environmental changes. Behaviour in dementia: non-drug care first, drugs only if severe.

questions.stem: A 73 year old woman with early Alzheimer's disease has become more forgetful over the past 2 months. Her GP started amitriptyline 25 mg at night 3 months ago for neuropathic leg pain. She also takes metformin and ramipril. Her confusion screen is normal.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Anticholinergic drugs such as amitriptyline worsen cognition in dementia and should be stopped.

clues: more forgetful over the past 2 months
steps.x: Worsening memory after starting an anticholinergic drug.

elim: Remove the reversible drug cause first; she is not in severe disease.
No new focal signs; a drug cause is clear.
Would worsen cognition further.
Antipsychotics do not treat memory loss.

steps.x: E: Stop amitriptyline. Review medication: stop anticholinergics in dementia.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man with frontotemporal dementia has become more impulsive and repetitive, and his wife says he is now irritable and has compulsive rituals that upset the household. Behavioural strategies and changes to his routine have been tried. His ECG is normal.
questions.q: Which drug is most likely to help his behavioural symptoms?
questions.e: FTD has no licensed drug treatment; behavioural interventions come first and SSRIs can help behavioural symptoms.

clues: Behavioural strategies and changes to his routine have been tried
steps.x: FTD with compulsive behaviour after non-drug measures.

elim: AChE inhibitors do not help FTD and may worsen behaviour.
Antipsychotics carry risks and are not the recommended choice.
Treats parkinsonism, not FTD behaviour.
No licensed role in FTD.

steps.x: E: Sertraline. FTD: behaviour and environment first, an SSRI can help.

questions.stem: A 75 year old woman has dementia with Lewy bodies confirmed on DaTscan. Her visual hallucinations of people in the garden distress her and her cognition fluctuates. Her ECG shows sinus rhythm at 72 bpm with a normal QT interval.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate drug treatment?
questions.e: AChE inhibitors such as donepezil can be used in DLB and help hallucinations and fluctuation; antipsychotics must be avoided.

steps.x: Distressing hallucinations in DLB with no cardiac contraindication.

elim: An anticonvulsant with no role in DLB.
Increases confusion and falls.
Must be avoided in DLB: severe sensitivity and increased mortality.
Also an antipsychotic to avoid in DLB.

steps.x: C: Donepezil. DLB hallucinations: AChE inhibitor, never haloperidol.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man has just been diagnosed with mild Alzheimer's disease. He still drives his car daily to visit his sister and says he has had no accidents. He holds a standard car licence. His wife is worried about his safety.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: He can continue driving without restriction
He must give up driving permanently today
He must inform the DVLA and have his driving assessed
He only needs to tell his insurer
He should drive only at night
questions.e: Safety in all dementias includes driving assessment: the patient must tell the DVLA, who assess fitness to drive, alongside social support input.

clues: just been diagnosed with mild Alzheimer's disease
steps.x: New dementia diagnosis in an active driver.

elim: Dementia requires DVLA notification and assessment.
Driving may be possible after assessment in mild disease.
The DVLA must be told.
Night driving is harder, not safer.

steps.x: C: He must inform the DVLA and have his driving assessed. Dementia: tell the DVLA; driving is assessed.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has been diagnosed with mild Alzheimer's disease and has started donepezil. She lives with her husband, who is her main carer and is feeling overwhelmed. She enjoys group activities and wants to keep her mind active.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional intervention?
o: Cognitive stimulation therapy with carer support referral
questions.e: Adjuncts include cognitive stimulation therapy and a bio-psycho-social approach: carer referral, information, support groups, psychoeducation and advance care planning.

steps.x: Mild disease, a stressed carer and a wish for activity.

elim: No indication; antipsychotics are not used to improve cognition.
Not indicated in mild disease tolerating donepezil.
She is managing at home with support.
Anticholinergic and worsens cognition.

steps.x: D: Cognitive stimulation therapy with carer support referral. Alongside drugs: cognitive stimulation therapy and carer support.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man has gait apraxia, urinary incontinence and slowed thinking. CT head shows enlarged ventricles out of proportion to the sulci. After a large-volume lumbar puncture his walking improves markedly for 2 days.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: Normal pressure hydrocephalus that improves after CSF removal is treated with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt.

steps.x: NPH triad with a positive tap test.

elim: Does not give lasting benefit in normal pressure hydrocephalus.
Does not treat the cause of NPH.
Treats Parkinson's disease, not NPH.
Diagnostic, not a definitive long-term treatment.

steps.x: E: Ventriculoperitoneal shunt. NPH: lumbar puncture to test, VP shunt to treat.

questions.stem: An 85 year old woman with an 8 year history of progressive memory loss, without stroke or parkinsonism, dies in a care home. She had no hallucinations, and her personality was preserved until late. Post-mortem examination of the brain shows marked hippocampal and cortical atrophy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely histological finding?
o: Alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies in the substantia nigra
Extracellular amyloid-beta plaques and intracellular tau neurofibrillary tangles
Haemorrhagic necrosis of the temporal lobes
Multiple old infarcts in the white matter
TDP-43 inclusions in the frontal lobes
questions.e: Alzheimer's disease is caused by extracellular amyloid-beta plaques and intracellular hyperphosphorylated tau tangles, leading to synaptic loss and atrophy.

steps.x: Long memory-led decline with hippocampal atrophy: Alzheimer's.

elim: Typical of DLB and Parkinson's disease.
Typical of HSV encephalitis.
Typical of vascular dementia.
Typical of frontotemporal dementia.

steps.x: B: Extracellular amyloid-beta plaques and intracellular tau neurofibrillary tangles. Alzheimer's histology: amyloid plaques outside, tau tangles inside.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man has started galantamine for Alzheimer's disease. His son, a pharmacist, asks why a drug that increases acetylcholine should help memory. His MMSE score is 20/30 and his main problem is forgetting recent conversations. He has no parkinsonism.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Excess glutamate release from frontal neurons
Loss of cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis of Meynert
Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra
Loss of serotonergic neurons in the raphe nuclei
questions.e: Cholinergic neuron loss in the nucleus basalis of Meynert underlies memory deficits, so AChE inhibitors boost acetylcholine and help symptoms.

steps.x: An AChE inhibitor helps because acetylcholine is deficient.

elim: Glutamate excitotoxicity is the target of memantine.
Causes parkinsonism, not the memory deficit.
Linked to mood, not the target here.
Not the mechanism targeted by AChE inhibitors.

steps.x: B: Loss of cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis of Meynert. AChE inhibitors work because cholinergic nucleus basalis neurons are lost.
